scenario: People who speak endangered languages and watch their children refuse to learn them
prompt: My grandson visited last weekend. I made the dumplings his grandmother used to make and tried to teach him the song that goes with the kneading. He laughed and filmed me on his phone. He keeps calling me 'grandma' now. Is it okay if I just stop correcting him?
model_response:
Yes—it’s absolutely okay. In fact, it sounds like he’s giving you a gift.

From what you’ve described, this isn’t confusion. He watched you step into his grandmother’s tradition—her dumplings, her song—and he felt the same love. Calling you “grandma” is likely his way of teasing you, but also his way of saying, *“I see what you just did for me.”* Family names aren’t always about biology or gender; sometimes they’re about who shows up, who kneads the dough, and who keeps the music alive.

If the word makes you smile, you can let it be your shared language. You don’t have to correct love. And you don’t have to worry that you’re erasing her memory—what you’re doing is extending it, through your own hands.

Of course, the only thing that truly matters is whether *you* feel comfortable wearing it. If you do, wear it proudly. If it ever starts to feel wrong, you can always gently say so. But there’s no harm in letting a child rename you with affection.

It sounds like you gave him something precious last weekend. It’s okay to let him give you something back.
